bollymeter.basis: Peaked at 21.5% nationwide (Nielsen Korea, Episode 13), averaged 18.3% across its run, and was extended by two episodes due to audience demand. Won Best Drama at the 2015 Hallyu Awards.

seasons.review_body: Yong-pal premiered on SBS in August 2015 and quickly became one of the year's dominant dramas, peaking at 21.5% nationwide ratings by Episode 13 - a figure that prompted SBS to extend the run by two episodes. The show's engine is a tension between its two halves: the first half operates as a kinetic medical thriller, with Kim Tae-hyun (Joo Won) navigating illegal house-calls to gangsters and corporate VIPs to keep his sister alive; the second half pivots into a chaebol revenge plot after the heiress Yeo-jin (Kim Tae-hee) awakens. The tonal shift from medical thriller to corporate revenge narrative is both the show's ambition and its main structural weakness - the kinetic energy of the early episodes was harder to sustain once the boardroom replaced the operating table. The lead performances held the two halves together, and the show's willingness to keep its stakes genuinely high gave it a pulse that more restrained romcoms of the era lacked.

# Yong Pal S1E1: "Episode 1" Review

*Spoiler-light verdict above. Full episode analysis below.*

The command comes before the explanation. Someone shouts for the car to stop, then the hour folds into a prayer about bad dreams and waking up. That is the pilot’s cleanest promise: escape will come through interruption, not comfort. By the time a wounded body appears outside the normal ER trail, the episode has turned that thought into machinery. The system looks for gangsters at nearby hospitals. Nothing. Someone asks for **Yong Pal**. The name arrives less like an introduction than a diagnosis.

## Wake Up or Bleed Out

The prayer segment gives the pilot its spine before the plot has finished showing its teeth. The way out of a bad dream, the episode says, is to wake up. Then the medical thriller begins proving how ugly waking up can be.

That opening idea matters because the hour keeps placing people inside systems that should protect them, then shows the gaps. After a fight, there are no suspicious patients reported at nearby ERs. Six hours pass inside the question the episode plants: if gangsters are hurt and no one has shown up at the obvious doors, where did they go? The answer arrives as need. Someone calls for Yong Pal because formal routes have failed or become too dangerous.

That is efficient pilot writing. The episode avoids explaining the legend too early. It starts with a practical absence. No patients. No reports. No visible trail. From that absence, the name gains force. The first episode works because it treats Yong Pal as a solution before it treats him as a character. The legend is what frightened people use when the hospital cannot be used.

## A Name That Leaves No ER Record

The medical beat that locks the premise into place is blunt: a doctor identifies “Spleen rupture.” There is no poetry in that line, and there should not be. The patient could bleed to death. The hour understands that urgency is cleaner than explanation. A ruptured spleen, missing ER records, and a whispered name do more for the premise than a long speech about underworld medicine could.

Then the hospital conversation lands the accusation: this is “definitely Yong Pal’s handiwork.” The phrasing carries more than one charge. Handiwork can suggest skill. It can also suggest evidence. It can sound like grudging respect or a charge sheet, depending on who says it. The pilot uses that ambiguity well. Yong Pal’s interventions leave people alive, and they leave a pattern other professionals can recognize.

That recognition is the episode’s first sharp craft move. It turns medicine into signature. A normal surgeon is known through credentials and hospital hierarchy. Yong Pal is known through the wound after he has touched it. The episode builds him through consequences: a patient who survived long enough to be argued over, a system that knows his mark, and an accusation waiting in the wings.

The risk is density. The dialogue-heavy stretches put a lot of premise on the table early, and some of it feels like paperwork being rushed through before the next emergency. Still, the core idea holds: the illegal doctor functions as a pressure valve.

## Permission Is Its Own Operating Table

The hospital section sharpens the contrast. In the OR, a resident is late or being checked, and third-year **Kim Tae-hyun** is not present yet. When he enters the hospital surgery context, the issue is his access as much as his skill. He wants permission or coverage to participate as a physician. That problem sits far from the back-channel call for Yong Pal.

The episode places two kinds of medicine beside each other. One moves through permission, rank, attendance, and institutional timing. The other moves because a body is collapsing and someone must act. During surgery, the blood pressure is given as 60 and urgent actions follow. The number gives the scene its clock. It also keeps the hospital material from becoming pure bureaucracy. The institution can be slow, but the OR still has real danger, procedure, and consequence.

That balance helps the pilot. Kim Tae-hyun’s late arrival and participation are more than a competence flex. The hour makes the friction procedural: who is allowed to do what, who covers whom, who gets checked, who is missing when the room needs hands. This is where the episode starts to earn its central conflict. A doctor can be necessary and still be out of position. A life-saving act can happen inside a system that will still ask whether the person had the right to perform it.

The weakness sits in the volume of dialogue. The pilot sometimes lets people explain pressure that the surgery already shows. Blood pressure at 60 is enough. The body is already making the argument.

## The Accusation Gives the Game Away

The confrontation around Yong Pal’s alleged extortion is the hour’s sharpest moral knot. An accuser charges that Yong Pal takes money and says the patient almost died before being saved. That wording matters. The accusation wants to discredit him, but it also admits the counterfactual. Without Yong Pal, the patient dies.

That contradiction is more interesting than a clean hero introduction. The episode asks what society does with a doctor whose methods sit outside the acceptable frame when the result is survival. Payment becomes the scandal. Survival becomes the uncomfortable evidence nobody can fully erase.

This is where the writing finds a harder edge. The patient almost dying is used against Yong Pal, even though the same detail proves the danger he faced. The accuser treats the payment as wrongdoing while leaning on the saved life as part of the complaint. That is messy in the right way. It makes the argument feel less like a courtroom point and more like resentment shaped into procedure.

The pilot could have flattened this into a Robin Hood doctor fantasy. Instead, it lets the charge remain ugly. Extortion is not softened. The money matters. The suspicion matters. But the episode also refuses to ignore the body on the table. A man lived. That fact keeps interrupting the moral lecture.

## A Sister in the Crossfire

The final stretch pushes the premise from professional risk into personal leverage. During the chase and standoff, the threat is direct: if they do not stop, “Then, my sister dies.” The line snaps the episode’s medical thriller machinery into family melodrama, but the connection works. Yong Pal’s skill can save strangers in gunshot chaos. It can also trap him when someone he loves is vulnerable.

That is a strong end point for a first episode. It takes the earlier question of who chooses whether the injured or shot boss stays alive without returning to the hospital and ties it to pressure outside medicine. The choice is no longer clinical. It is coercive. The body that needs saving becomes leverage over another body offscreen.

The hour also plants a separate power struggle around **Chairman** and **Ms. Young Ae**, specifically through patient visitation and refusal. The pilot leaves that thread unresolved, and the material is thinner in this episode than the Yong Pal material. It functions more as a locked door than a full dramatic engine. Still, the placement matters. Hospital access, refusal, permission, and secrecy are central conditions in this world.

The chase works because it makes the episode’s title dangerous. Being the person people call can make a doctor valuable. It can also make him impossible to release.

## The Verdict

“Episode 1” is a muscular pilot with a clean hook: a doctor defined by the lives he saves outside the routes that respectable medicine can admit. Its strongest material comes from contradiction. Yong Pal is accused through the same facts that prove his usefulness. Kim Tae-hyun’s hospital world runs on permission while the emergency world runs on blood loss and fear. The episode’s weaker habit is overloading dialogue when the physical details already carry the scene, especially in the institutional stretches. But the opening prayer, the missing ER trail, the ruptured spleen, the OR pressure, and the sister threat all point in the same direction. As a season starter, it plants enough medical, criminal, and family pressure to make the next episode feel necessary.

Written by BollyAI, reviewed by our editorial team.
